paragraph.text: the "but" reveals the contradiction. Loving some animals while paying for others, just as able to suffer, to be killed is what psychology calls the meat paradox. The sentence isn't an argument: it's the description of a conflict between what the person values and what they do. And that conflict is actually the best starting point for change.
"I have three dogs. I'm an animal lover, but I won't give up meat."
I love and care for several animals.
Eating meat is a separate practice, tied to food rather than affection.
I can love animals and eat meat without contradiction, as many people do.
So eating meat doesn't contradict my love of animals.
P1 is sincere. The problem lies in P2 and P3: the split between animals "for affection" and animals "for food" doesn't correspond to any difference in the animals themselves.
fails at P2, which treats a category created by habit as a real difference.
"I'm an animal lover, but I won't give up meat."
"I rescue cats and I eat barbecue; what's the problem?"
"It's natural to put our own first." (which is A13)

Imagine someone who says: "I really love my classmates, but I push some of them." Strange, right? If we love animals, it makes sense to think about whether the pig and the chicken also deserve that love. They feel fear and pain just like the dog at home.

Loving animals is real and a great start. But pigs, cows and chickens feel pain and fear like the dogs and cats you love. The difference between them isn't in the animals, but in the place habit has given each one. Psychology calls this the meat paradox. If the love of animals is sincere, it's the best reason to extend that care to those on the plate.
"What does a pig have that's different from your dog that justifies eating one and loving the other?"
The sentence puts together a value and a practice that pull in opposite directions:
Pays for practices that make animals suffer
Caring for the animals at home
Funds the slaughter of others with similar capacities
Accepts practices that would be cruelty if done to dogs

text.bold: 1. The difference is in the habit, not the animal.

paragraph.text: Pigs, cows and chickens feel pain and fear like dogs and cats. Comparisons of intelligence between species are imprecise, and not even needed: what matters is the capacity to suffer. The split between "pet" and "food" is cultural: in other countries, different animals sit on each side.

Psychology has studied this conflict for over a decade. Research shows people attribute less mind and less moral status to the animals they eat, and do so more when reminded of the link between meat and suffering.
In one experiment, classifying an animal as food was enough to lower the moral status attributed to it. The animal doesn't change; the way we see it does.
The sentence isn't a defense; it's the recognition of a conflict. Those who love animals already accept the most important premise: that they matter.
After the "but" usually comes taste (J11), custom (D1) or priority (A13). Those are the arguments that need examining.
Eating meat reduces the moral status and mind attributed to animals
A classic study on the meat paradox
Being reminded of the link between meat and suffering increases the denial of mind to animals
Classifying an animal as food lowers the moral status attributed to it
(d) The strongest counter-reply: love is always partial
The most serious version says all love is partial: we love our family more than strangers, and no one finds that contradictory. Loving one's own animals more than others would be equally natural.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
We love our family more than strangers, but we don't pay for strangers to suffer (A13).
Not caring for everyone is different from funding the suffering of some.

text.bold: The counter-reply concedes the central point.

paragraph.text: If the issue is just how intensely one loves, the other animals still deserve, at least, not to be harmed.
A13 "It's natural to put our own first"
E12 "I know it's wrong, but I won't change"
Admits the contradiction and doesn't change
The difference between "pet" and "food" isn't in the animals
Keeps affection and consumption in separate boxes
Values animal welfare and funds the opposite

text.bold: Would be horrified if someone ate their dog.

paragraph.text: But accepts eating animals with similar capacities.
And funds practices that would be cruelty if done to dogs.
The sentence already contains the contradiction.
The conflict is reduced by denying minds to food animals
"Food" and "companion" seem like different kinds of animal
Being reminded of suffering leads to attributing less mind
The principle being tested is: "I can love one category of beings and fund the suffering of another similar one".
Dogs and cats in other countries
Eating them would be acceptable for someone who has other dogs
Those who say this usually condemn it
Loving one's own family would license exploiting strangers
They'd be loved at home and eaten on the farm

Loving animals is sincere and valuable. People who care for dogs and cats, rescue animals or are outraged by cruelty already show that animals matter to them. That affection is a real force, not hypocrisy.

What the sentence reveals isn't an excuse but a conflict. And conflicts like this are often the beginning of change: all it takes is extending the same love to the animals still on the other side of the line.
